did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ezekiel is commanded to shave his head and beard with a sharp razor, and then weigh and divide the hair on a scale. This symbolic act begins the description of Jerusalem’s fate.

Did you know? The hair is divided into three parts: one-third is burned in the fire, one-third is struck with the sword around the city, and one-third is scattered to the wind; even after the last third, a sword is sent.
Did you know? From the scattered hair, Ezekiel is commanded to take a few strands and bind them in the folds of his garment, symbolizing a small remnant preserved from the calamity.
Did you know? Even from the bound remnant, another portion is taken and thrown into the fire; from that fire, a fire will spread to the whole house of Israel.
Did you know? The LORD presents Jerusalem as a city set among the nations, with many countries surrounding it. Its central location emphasizes its importance and the responsibility placed upon it.
Did you know? According to the chapter, Jerusalem rebelled against the LORD’s judgments and laws, and did not even follow properly the ways of the nations around it.

Did you know? Because of Jerusalem’s sins, the LORD says that He will execute judgment in its midst in the sight of the nations; the punishment is presented as an event that will also be seen by the surrounding peoples.
Did you know? The chapter describes extreme famine within Jerusalem, to the point that fathers and sons will eat one another; afterward, the survivors will also be scattered to every wind.

Did you know? The fate of Jerusalem’s inhabitants is again divided into three parts: one-third will die by plague and famine, one-third will fall by the sword around the city, and one-third will be scattered to every wind while the sword pursues them.
Did you know? Famine is described as deadly arrows sent to destroy, and its practical expression is the breaking of the ‘staff of bread’—the source of a person’s food and support.
